newsitem.title: USA: No sign Canada to curb disputed U.S. wheat sales.
newsitem.headline: No sign Canada to curb disputed U.S. wheat sales.

text.p: Canadian officials gave no signs they would curb wheat shipments into the U.S. market, Commerce Secretary William Daley said Thursday, but he hoped for progress in a salmon dispute between the two countries.

Both issues were aired during meetings this week with officials from the provincial and national level. Despite the rancour surrounding them, Daley said there was "no better trading relationship in the world" than the United States and Canada, where trade amounts to $1 billion a day.
Speaking to reporters by telephone from Vancouver, Daley said, "No, they did not," when asked if Canadian officials indicated they would scale back on wheat shipments.
Some farmers and lawmakers from the Wheat Belt have called for a halt to all imports of Canadian wheat. They contend Canadian wheat has depressed U.S. prices and undercut farm viability.
Canadian officials have stoutly defended the sales as even-handed deals and reject suggestions of "dumping" -- selling grain at unfairly low prices.

In fall 1994, the nations agreed to a one-year limit on Canadian shipments of 1.5 million metric tons. The agreement was not renewed but farm-state demands for action have escalated since recent shipments have breached that level.
Daley said he discussed with Canadian officials the dispute over salmon fishing limits off the U.S. and Canadian West Coasts. Each side has accused the other of depleting stocks.
With the appointment of special envoys from each country, Daley said he was "hopeful" that negotiations "will begin to make progress" when talks resume in the fall.

The Commerce Department has begun gathering information to decide whether an antidumping investigation would be warranted on wheat. Daley declined to suggest when the research stage would end. Asked if the department would initiate a complaint, he said, "That's a decision you make after you gather information."
